query: For CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys (X = Si, Mn, or Al) in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain whether a stable, coherent protective oxide layer forms and persists during exposure above 900 °C in an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere, rather than developing unstable surface oxides that crack or spall? Specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison against a defined baseline, the predicted differences, the applicable exposure and material-state boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a falsifying observation.

generation.hypothesis: In CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys, the element X controls the formation and persistence of a protective oxide layer at temperatures above 900 °C by tuning the balance between thermodynamically-favored selective oxidation and the kinetic barriers imposed by interfacial diffusion. Specifically, when X is an element like Al or Si, its incorporation promotes the nucleation of slow-growing, coherent oxides (e.g., Al2O3 or SiO2, possibly in combination with Cr2O3) that form an effective diffusion barrier, whereas when X is Mn, its high diffusivity and lower oxide adhesion lead to rapid formation of nonprotective, spall-prone manganese oxides.
generation.material_initial_state: CrFeCoNiX alloys in single or multiphase metallic solid-solution state prepared with identical processing history
generation.intervention: Systematic substitution of the X element among Al, Si, and Mn, with a control sample of CrFeCoNi (without X)
generation.conditions: Exposure at temperatures above 900 °C in a controlled oxidative or corrosive atmosphere for sustained durations (e.g., 100 h or more)
generation.structural_mediator: The nature and microstructure of the oxide scale formed at the alloy/oxide interface (e.g., oxide phase composition, scale thickness, and adhesion/coherence)
generation.mechanism: The alloying addition X alters the selective oxidation pathway via its inherent oxidation affinity and diffusion kinetics. In alloys with Al or Si, the slower diffusion and high thermodynamic stability of formed oxides favor the development of a thin, coherent, and self-healing oxide barrier. In contrast, Mn promotes the formation of a rapid but poorly adherent oxide scale that develops cracks or spalls due to high diffusion rates and inadequate scale cohesion.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared with the baseline CrFeCoNi alloy, the Al- and Si-containing alloys will form thinner, more adherent and coherent oxide scales with lower overall mass gain during oxidation, while the Mn-containing alloy will exhibit thicker, less coherent oxide scales with increased spallation and higher mass gain.
generation.baseline: CrFeCoNi alloy without an added X element
generation.boundary: Results are expected under high-temperature oxidation/corrosion conditions (>900 °C) while maintaining the alloys in a controlled single- or multiphase solid-solution state; deviations may occur if microstructure or processing variances become dominant.
generation.uncertainty: Exact quantitative differences (e.g., oxide thickness or mass gain) between the alloys are uncertain due to potential interplay between microstructural factors (e.g., grain size, phase distribution) and elemental diffusion processes. The relative contributions of thermodynamic driving forces versus kinetic diffusion barriers require further elucidation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloy samples where X is systematically varied among Al, Si, and Mn along with a baseline CrFeCoNi sample. Ensure identical processing to achieve comparable microstructures. Subject all samples to a high-temperature oxidation/corrosion test at >900 °C (e.g., 100 h exposure) in a controlled atmosphere.
measurements: Quantify mass gain during oxidation (thermogravimetric analysis)
Determine oxide phase composition and morphology (XRD, SEM-EDS)
Assess oxide scale adhesion and coherence (scratch testing or in situ imaging)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Al- and Si-alloyed samples do not consistently show thinner, more coherent, protective oxide scales (with lower mass gain) relative to both the Mn-alloyed and baseline CrFeCoNi samples, then the hypothesis that X controls oxide stability via a balance between selective oxidation and kinetic diffusion barriers is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: This paper utilizes in situ X-ray diffraction (XRD) to investigate the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy (HEA). We found that (1) Mn is the major oxide-forming element in both vacuum and air environments, leading to the formation of non-protective oxides that deplete the bulk alloy of Mn; (2) no oxides like Cr 2 O 3 , Fe 2 O 3 , or Fe 3 O 4 were observed during the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi, which contradicts some previous studies on the isothermal oxidation of CrMnFeCoNi HEA. We also analysed and compared the experimental results with thermodynamic calculations by using ThermoCalc version 2022b software following the CALPHAD method. ThermoCalc predicted spinel oxide in a vacuum environment, along with halite oxides observed in experimental results; also, in an atmospheric environment, it predicted only spinel, indicating the need for further investigation into factors to validate the thermodynamic predictions. Abstract This work investigates the effect of ultrafine-grain microstructure on the oxidation behavior of AlCoCrFeNi high entropy alloy (HEA). The ultrafine-grain microstructure is obtained using stationary friction processing performed at two different rotational speeds, 400 and 1800 rpm, for 5 min duration. Processed samples demonstrate high depth of refinement (DOR) and ultrafine grain size (0.43–1 μm) at high rotational speeds along with significant phase transformations from BCC/B2 to FCC microstructure. Further, surface free energy of the ultrafine-grain microstructure is enhanced up to 35%. Oxidation kinetics of the ultrafine-grained sample is decelerated up to 12–48% in a temperature range of 850–1050 °C for a duration of 100 h. Chromia and alumina were the predominant oxides formed in almost all the samples oxidized at elevated temperature. In addition, spinel Co(Cr,Fe) 2 O 4 /Fe(Co,Cr) 2 O 4 formation is also detected in the unprocessed oxidized samples. Processed samples rich in grain boundaries (GBs) promote internal oxidation to form Al-rich inner oxides. frame.system: CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys, with X = Si, Mn, or Al, in either a single‐phase or multiphase metallic solid-solution state
frame.goal: To understand the mechanistic conditions that govern whether a stable, coherent protective oxide layer (such as Cr2O3 or Al2O3) forms and persists at temperatures above 900 °C in oxidative/corrosive atmospheres, rather than developing unstable, cracked/spalled oxides.
frame.limitation: There is uncertainty about which specific elemental contributions (e.g., role of X in modifying oxidation kinetics, phase stability, and diffusion behavior) and microstructural factors control the transition from forming protective oxide films to the development of unstable, spall-prone surface oxides.
root_cause_cues: stable, coherent protective oxide layer forms and persists
unstable surface oxides that crack or spall
constraints: Must propose a single, testable mechanistic hypothesis
Need to specify what governs the behavior (e.g., thermodynamics, kinetics, elemental diffusion)
A controlled comparison is required against a defined baseline alloy (for example, a CrFeCoNi alloy without the X element or one with a different X)
The hypothesis must outline predicted differences under well-defined exposure (above 900 °C) and material-state boundaries
Supporting prior evidence (e.g., prior work on oxidation behavior of high-entropy alloys or related systems) must be cited
A falsifying observation must be identified that would disprove the proposed mechanism
frame.regime: High-temperature exposure (>900 °C) in oxidative/corrosive atmospheres, where the alloy is maintained in a single- or multiphase solid-solution state.
prior_attempts: Comparisons between baseline CrFeCoNi alloys and variants with added X elements have been made in past studies without a unified mechanistic theory, leaving open questions about how specific elemental additions shift oxidation kinetics, oxide phase stability, or diffusion barriers.

Previous work has examined oxidation rates and oxide scale morphologies, yet failed to provide a single hypothesis that correlates alloying chemistry with the transformation from protective to unstable oxide growth under extreme conditions.

decision.trend: Early studies of high‐entropy alloy oxidation focused first on documenting the high‐temperature kinetics and oxide “morphologies” in refractory or multiphase systems, observing that factors such as ultrafine grains (which increase the density of fast diffusion paths) or elemental segregation strongly affected whether a protective scale (like Al2O3 or Cr2O3) formed. For example, PMC9026100 demonstrated that an ultrafine-grained AlCoCrFeNi alloy favored formation of coherent, protective oxides, while PMC10384371 on a CrMnFeCoNi alloy revealed that excessive diffusion of Mn led to nonprotective, unstable oxide mixes. Although these works highlighted that elemental additions (and associated diffusion kinetics) are key, no single mechanistic hypothesis has yet unified how the choice of an added element (“X” = Si, Mn, or Al) alters the balance between the thermodynamic driving forces and kinetic diffusion barriers that ultimately dictate scale coherence under >900 °C oxidative/corrosive conditions.
decision.unsolved: It remains unclear which specific role the added element (X) plays in altering the interfacial diffusion kinetics and phase stability of the growing oxide layer. In particular, how the modification of elemental diffusivities and selective oxidation behavior by Si, Mn, or Al shifts the transition from protective (coherent, adherent Cr2O3/Al2O3 layers) to unstable scale (cracked or spalled oxides) has not been resolved. A unified, testable hypothesis linking these chemical and microstructural factors to oxide scale integrity under defined high‐temperature exposure conditions is still needed.
decision.lever: Systematic variation of the X element in CrFeCoNiX alloys (by comparing a baseline CrFeCoNi alloy with otherwise identical alloys containing Si, Mn, or Al) while carefully quantifying oxide scale growth kinetics, diffusion profiles, and microstructural evolution under >900 °C oxidative/corrosive conditions.
decision.why: Because previous work has separately shown that grain refinement and elemental segregation can promote the formation of protective oxides (when Al is present) or cause nonprotective oxidation (when Mn dominates), a controlled experiment that varies only the X element will directly test the hypothesis that the balance between selective oxidation (governed by thermodynamic preferences) and diffusion barrier formation (governed by kinetic parameters) controls scale integrity. This approach builds on prior observations and directly addresses the open question of how specific elemental contributions modulate the transition from protective to spall-prone oxide behavior.
